title: US College Disability Reporting Doubles to 46% as Mental Health Drives Surge at Elite Campuses
text: US College Disability Reporting Doubles to 46% as Mental Health Drives Surge at Elite Campuses Federal data reveals that over 46 percent of US colleges now report significant disability rates, driven by mental health conditions. Selective institutions show the highest concentrations of students with registered disabilities. More than 46 percent of US higher-education institutions reported that at least 3 percent of their undergraduates had a registered disability in fall 2023. This figure represents a dramatic increase from 2008, when the federal government first began tracking these specific enrollment metrics. The surge indicates a widespread acceleration in how students access formal support systems across the United States. Highly selective colleges with admissions rates below 20 percent are far more likely to enroll large shares of students with disabilities. Seven out of ten such institutions exceeded the 10 percent disability threshold in 2023. This stands in stark contrast to the national average of only 32 percent of institutions nationwide reaching that same level.Mental-health conditions and attention-deficit disorder now account for roughly 70 percent of all students with reported disabilities. A 2024 Government Accountability Office report confirmed the share of undergraduates with disabilities nearly doubled from 11 percent in 2004 to 21 percent in 2020. Behavioral or emotional conditions rose significantly during this period, reflecting profound changes in student health needs.Stanford University saw its share of students with disabilities more than double from 17 percent in 2018 to 38 percent in 2023. Institutions designed specifically for students with learning differences, such as Landmark College, have consistently topped the list of highest disability shares. These findings challenge assumptions about accessibility being limited to less competitive schools.A separate survey by the National Disability Center for Student Success estimates that 43 percent of undergraduates actually have a disability. However, fewer than half, specifically 47 percent, disclose it to their university. This significant gap suggests that official statistics capture only a fraction of the actual demand for accommodations and services on campus.Stephanie W. Cawthon, executive director of the National Disability Center for Student Success, described the post-pandemic rise in anxiety and depression as alarmingly high. She noted that these levels are beyond what campuses anticipated when preparing their support infrastructure. The data suggests institutional readiness has not kept pace with the rapid expansion of these specific needs.Some stakeholders question the legitimacy of the increase and worry it reflects system abuse rather than genuine need. There are concerns that accommodations are being exploited, potentially undermining academic standards and straining campus resources. Cawthon argues that for every student gaming the system, there are nine who are not seeking unfair advantages.Colleges must navigate these competing pressures while ensuring equitable access for all students requiring support. The shift requires disability-services offices to manage caseloads dominated by mental-health needs rather than physical disabilities. This demands different expertise, staffing models, and partnerships with counseling centers across higher education.Institutions designed for universal learning and accessible design may reduce the need for individualized accommodations over time. The trend of increased mental-health disclosure among Gen Z points to continued growth in reporting. Universities that invest in proactive support structures will be better positioned than those treating current levels as a ceiling.

Highly selective colleges with admissions rates below 20 percent are far more likely to enroll large shares of students with disabilities. Institutions designed specifically for students with learning differences, such as Landmark College, have consistently topped the list of highest disability shares.
